body.heading: Stronger than the ingredients
paragraphs: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements — usually other metals, sometimes a non-metal like carbon — melted or fused together so the atoms mingle. The point of mixing is that the blend beats the ingredients: pure copper is soft, pure iron rusts and bends, and pure gold can be dented with a fingernail's worth of force, but their alloys are the working metals of civilisation.

The reason is geometry. In a pure metal, layers of identical atoms slide over each other fairly easily, which is why pure metals are soft. Mix in atoms of a different size and the layers jam against the intruders — sliding becomes hard work, and the metal becomes harder and stronger.

body.heading: Three famous blends
paragraphs: Bronze came first: copper with about a tenth tin, hard enough for swords, tools and statues, and so important it named an age of history. Brass — copper with zinc — is easier to shape, resists corrosion, and rings brightly, which is why it ends up in instruments, taps and door handles.

Steel is the giant: iron with a small amount of carbon, typically well under two percent. That pinch of carbon transforms soft iron into the skeleton of bridges and skyscrapers. Add chromium as well and you get stainless steel, which resists rust; add other metals in careful recipes and you get steels for springs, drills and jet engines.

body.heading: Mixing with intent
paragraphs: Modern alloys are designed the way chefs develop recipes, except the testing is done with computers and electron microscopes. Aircraft bodies use aluminium alloys that keep aluminium's lightness while borrowing strength from copper, magnesium or zinc. Jewellers alloy gold with copper or silver because a ring of pure gold would wear away and bend.

Even the fillings once used in teeth were an alloy — amalgam, a mix involving mercury — and the solder joining your electronics is one too. Whenever a single metal is almost right, an alloy usually finishes the job.

description: Bronze, brass and steel are not elements but mixtures — metals blended on purpose because the mix outperforms any single metal in it.
